marrow__ANAT_CH08_Q001.takeaway: Facial development uses frontonasal, paired maxillary and paired mandibular prominences; there is no embryologic zygomatic prominence.
marrow__ANAT_CH08_Q001.displayText:
Zygomatic prominence is not an embryologic structure that contributes to the formation of the face.

The face is derived from the following structures around the stomatodeum (primitive mouth):
• Mandibular prominences and maxillary prominences of the first arch
• Frontonasal prominence formed by the proliferation of mesenchyme ventral to the brain vesicles. It also gives rise to medial and lateral nasal prominences.

The source table lists the prominences contributing to facial development and the structures formed from them.

rationales.a: The frontonasal prominence is a true facial prominence and contributes to the forehead and bridge of the nose while generating the nasal prominences.
rationales.c: The maxillary prominences are first-arch derivatives that form the upper cheek and lateral portions of the upper lip.
rationales.d: The mandibular prominences are first-arch derivatives that form the lower cheek, lower lip and chin.

marrow__ANAT_CH08_Q002.takeaway: The upper lip forms by fusion of the maxillary prominences with the medial nasal prominences.
marrow__ANAT_CH08_Q002.displayText:
The upper lip is formed by the fusion of the two maxillary prominences with the two medial nasal prominences.

Initially, two thickenings called nasal placodes are formed in the frontonasal prominence. The nasal placodes get depressed to become nasal pits. Each nasal pit has a ridge of tissue on the outer edge called lateral nasal prominence and on the inner edge called medial nasal prominence.

The two maxillary prominences on the lateral part of the stomatodeum increase in size and grow medially. They compress the medial nasal prominences toward the midline. Later, the two maxillary prominences fuse with the two medial nasal prominences to form the upper lip.

rationales.a: The mandibular prominences form the lower lip and chin, so they do not combine with the maxillary prominences to form the upper lip.
rationales.c: Lateral nasal prominences form the alae of the nose rather than the medial component of the upper lip.
rationales.d: Although the medial nasal prominences contribute to the upper lip, mandibular prominences contribute to the lower lip and chin, not the upper lip.

marrow__ANAT_CH08_Q003.takeaway: The alae of the nose are derived from the lateral nasal processes.
marrow__ANAT_CH08_Q003.displayText:
The alae of the nose develop from the lateral nasal processes.

The development of various components of the nose can be summarized as follows:
• Bridge - The frontonasal process
• Dorsum and tip - Fused medial nasal processes
• Alae - The lateral nasal processes
• Anterior nares (nostrils) - The original site of the nasal pit
• Nasal cavity - The nasal sacs formed by the elongation of nasal pits
• Posterior nares (choanae) - Ruptured bucconasal membrane

rationales.a: The frontonasal process contributes to the bridge of the nose rather than the alae.
rationales.b: The medial nasal processes contribute to the dorsum and tip of the nose and the intermaxillary segment, not the alae.
rationales.d: The bucconasal membrane is related to formation of the posterior nares after rupture; it does not form the alae.

marrow__ANAT_CH08_Q004.takeaway: A typical cleft lip results from failure of fusion between the maxillary prominence and medial nasal prominence.
marrow__ANAT_CH08_Q004.displayText:
The image shows cleft lip which occurs when the maxillary prominences fail to fuse with the medial nasal prominences.

Various defects of fusion of prominences in the face region are as follows:
• A cleft lip is due to the failure of the fusion of maxillary prominence with medial nasal prominence. It can be unilateral or bilateral. It can vary in severity from a small notch in the upper lip to a double cleft extending into both the nostrils. There is also associated underdevelopment of the part of the maxilla that bears the incisors.
• Median (midline) cleft lip is a rare defect occurring due to failure of the two medial nasal prominences to fuse in the midline.
• The oblique facial cleft is caused by the failure of the maxillary prominence to fuse with the lateral nasal prominence along the line of the nasolacrimal groove. The nasolacrimal duct is exposed to the surface in these cases.

rationales.a: The mandibular prominence does not fuse with the lateral nasal prominence to form the upper lip, so this pairing does not explain the pictured cleft lip.
rationales.b: Failure of maxillary prominence to fuse with the lateral nasal prominence causes an oblique facial cleft along the nasolacrimal groove, not a typical cleft lip.
rationales.c: The mandibular prominence forms lower facial structures and its fusion with a medial nasal prominence is not the developmental event that forms the upper lip.

marrow__ANAT_CH08_Q005.takeaway: The primary palate is the palatal component of the intermaxillary segment formed by fusion of the two medial nasal prominences.
marrow__ANAT_CH08_Q005.displayText:
The primary palate (premaxilla) develops from the intermaxillary segment that is formed by the fusion of the two medial nasal prominences.

The intermaxillary segment has the following components:
• Labial component - forms the philtrum of the upper lip
• Upper jaw component - forms the medial part of the maxillary bone with the four upper incisor teeth
• Palatal component - forms the triangular area in the front called the primary palate (premaxilla)

rationales.b: Lateral nasal prominences principally form the alae of the nose and do not generate the intermaxillary segment or primary palate.
rationales.c: Maxillary prominences give rise to the palatine shelves that form the secondary palate, not the primary palate.
rationales.d: The frontonasal prominence gives rise to the nasal prominences, but the immediate paired structures whose fusion forms the intermaxillary segment are the medial nasal prominences.

marrow__ANAT_CH08_Q006.takeaway: Bilateral complete cleft palate requires failure of palatine shelves to fuse both with each other and with the premaxilla.
marrow__ANAT_CH08_Q006.displayText:
Bilateral complete cleft palate is due to the non-fusion of palatine processes with the premaxilla and with each other.

The palate is formed from two main structures:
• Primary palate: The small triangular anterior part of the palate is formed by the fused medial nasal processes (intermaxillary segment or premaxilla).
• Secondary palate: The main part of the palate is formed by the two palatine processes that converge from the maxillary processes.

The cleft palate can occur in the primary palate (anterior cleft) or in the secondary palate (posterior palate).
• Complete cleft palate involves both the primary and secondary palate.
• Incomplete cleft palate involves only the secondary palate.
In bilateral complete cleft palate, a Y-shaped cleft is seen with gaps between the primary and secondary palate and between the two halves of the secondary palate. In addition, there is a bilateral cleft upper lip.

rationales.a: Failure only between the palatine processes and premaxilla does not account for the additional midline separation between the two palatine processes in a complete bilateral cleft.
rationales.b: Failure only of midline palatine-process fusion affects the secondary palate but does not explain extension through the primary-secondary palate junction.
rationales.d: Failure of medial nasal-maxillary fusion produces cleft lip; it is not the complete palatal fusion defect described here.

marrow__ANAT_CH08_Q007.takeaway: The nasolacrimal duct is ectodermal, developing from an epithelial cord in the nasolacrimal groove.
marrow__ANAT_CH08_Q007.displayText:
The nasolacrimal duct is derived from the ectoderm of the nasolacrimal groove (also known as naso-optic furrow).

The deep furrow between the maxillary and lateral nasal prominence is known as the nasolacrimal groove.
• The ectoderm in the floor of this groove becomes a solid epithelial cord and detaches from the overlying ectoderm.
• This solid cord then canalizes to form the nasolacrimal duct.
• The lower end of the duct acquires a connection to the nasal cavity.
• The upper end of the duct widens to form the lacrimal sac.

rationales.b: Mesoderm contributes connective and vascular tissues but is not the epithelial origin of the nasolacrimal duct.
rationales.c: Endoderm does not contribute to the nasolacrimal duct; its epithelial primordium is ectodermal.
rationales.d: Although surrounding mesenchyme supports development, the duct itself arises from ectoderm rather than a mixed ectoderm-mesoderm origin.

marrow__ANAT_CH08_Q008.takeaway: Eye development proceeds in the sequence optic sulcus → optic vesicle → optic stalk → optic cup.
marrow__ANAT_CH08_Q008.displayText: The earliest recognizable event in this sequence is the optic sulcus in forebrain neuroectoderm. It evaginates to form the optic vesicle, which remains connected to the forebrain by the optic stalk. Invagination of the optic vesicle then produces the double-walled optic cup. The reconstructed list is 1. Optic vesicle; 2. Optic stalk; 3. Optic cup; 4. Optic sulcus, giving the source-keyed sequence 4-1-2-3. The original question page omits the numbered legend; these labels are reconstructed by combining the four-stage order in the source explanation with the printed answer key, rather than transcribed from an original on-page list.

rationales.a: Sequence 1-2-3-4 does not match the authoritative developmental order keyed in the source.
rationales.b: Sequence 2-4-3-1 does not match the authoritative developmental order keyed in the source.
rationales.d: Sequence 1-3-4-2 does not match the authoritative developmental order keyed in the source.

marrow__ANAT_CH08_Q009.takeaway: Coloboma results from failure of closure of the embryonic choroid fissure; distal failure can involve the iris.
marrow__ANAT_CH08_Q009.displayText:
The condition coloboma of the iris occurs due to failure of the choroid fissure to close in the distal part forming a cleft.

There is a small gap in the inferior surface of the optic cup known as the choroid fissure. This fissure allows the hyaloid vessels to reach the inner chamber of the eye. During the normal development of the eye, the distal part of the hyaloid artery degenerates. The choroid fissure then fuses and this makes the mouth of the optic cup into a round opening (the future pupil).

Failure of fusion of choroid fissure causes clefts in the eye known as coloboma.
• If the failure to fuse is in the distal part, it can result in coloboma of the iris.
• If the failure of fusion occurs in the proximal part, it can lead to coloboma of the retina/choroid/optic nerve, depending on the location of the defect.

rationales.a: Congenital retinal detachment is not the embryologic closure defect responsible for the characteristic iris cleft of coloboma.
rationales.b: Formation of the posterior chamber is unrelated to persistence of the inferior embryonic fissure that causes coloboma.
rationales.c: Neural crest contributes important ocular connective tissues, but iris coloboma specifically reflects failure of choroid-fissure closure.

marrow__ANAT_CH08_Q010.takeaway: Sphincter pupillae and dilator pupillae are unusual muscles derived from neuroectoderm of the optic cup.
marrow__ANAT_CH08_Q010.displayText:
The musculature of the iris, including the sphincter pupillae and dilator pupillae, are derived from the ectoderm of the optic cup.

Most of the muscles of the body develop from mesoderm. The muscles which develop from ectoderm are:
• Muscles of the iris (sphincter and dilator pupillae)
• Arrectores pilorum of skin
• Myoepithelial cells lining the ducts of sweat glands

rationales.b: Endoderm forms epithelial linings and parenchyma of several organs but does not form the intrinsic muscles of the iris.
rationales.c: Most skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle is mesodermal, but sphincter and dilator pupillae are a classic ectodermal exception.
rationales.d: Neural crest contributes ocular stromal structures but is not the source of the sphincter and dilator pupillae in this question.

marrow__ANAT_CH08_Q011.takeaway: The auricle develops from six hillocks contributed by the first and second pharyngeal arches; defects can cause anotia.
marrow__ANAT_CH08_Q011.displayText:
Anotia (complete absence of the ear pinna) occurs due to the defect in the development of 1st and 2nd pharyngeal arches.

The pinna develops from 6 tissue elevations called the auricular hillocks formed around the margins of the dorsal portion of the 1st pharyngeal cleft.
• 3 hillocks arise from the 1st pharyngeal (mandibular) arch
• 3 hillocks are from the 2nd pharyngeal (hyoid) arch

The mandibular arch contributes to the tragus of the pinna only, while the rest of the pinna is derived from the hyoid arch. Invagination of the first pharyngeal arch gives rise to the external auditory meatus.

Previously, it was believed that the external auditory meatus develops from the first pharyngeal cleft. But recent studies suggest that the first pharyngeal arch gives rise to the external auditory meatus.

rationales.a: The third and fourth arches contribute other pharyngeal derivatives and do not provide the six auricular hillocks that form the pinna.
rationales.b: The second arch contributes to the pinna, but the third arch does not replace the essential first-arch contribution.
rationales.d: The first arch contributes to the auricle, but the third arch is not the partner arch; the remaining hillocks arise from the second arch.

marrow__ANAT_CH08_Q012.takeaway: The tympanic membrane uniquely contains contributions from ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm.
marrow__ANAT_CH08_Q012.displayText:
The tympanic membrane is derived from all three germ layers.

The tympanic membrane is formed by the apposition of the tubotympanic recess of the 1st pharyngeal pouch with the 1st pharyngeal cleft.
• The outer layer of the tympanic membrane is derived from the ectoderm at the bottom of the external auditory meatus (1st pharyngeal cleft).
• The inner layer of the tympanic membrane is derived from the endoderm lining the tympanic cavity (1st pharyngeal pouch).
• The middle layer of the tympanic membrane is connective tissue derived from the mesoderm.

rationales.a: The auditory ossicles arise from pharyngeal-arch mesenchyme and do not contain direct contributions from all three germ layers.
rationales.b: The external acoustic meatus is derived from the first-cleft/first-arch ectodermal region rather than all three germ layers.
rationales.c: The middle-ear cavity and auditory tube are lined by endoderm from the first pharyngeal pouch; they are not themselves three-germ-layer structures.

marrow__ANAT_CH08_Q013.takeaway: The tubotympanic recess of the first pharyngeal pouch forms the middle-ear cavity and auditory (Eustachian) tube.
marrow__ANAT_CH08_Q013.displayText:
The tubotympanic recess forms the auditory tube.

Development of the middle ear:
• The distal part of the 1st pharyngeal pouch becomes the tubotympanic recess. The tubotympanic recess gives rise to the primitive tympanic cavity distally, while the proximal part remains narrow and forms the auditory tube (eustachian tube). It also forms the lining of the middle ear cavity.
• The 3 ossicles are formed from mesenchymal condensations from the 1st pharyngeal arch (malleus and incus) and 2nd pharyngeal arch (stapes).
• The tympanic membrane is formed where the ectoderm of the 1st pharyngeal cleft dips to meet the endoderm of the 1st pharyngeal pouch, with contribution from the intervening mesoderm.

rationales.b: The external auditory meatus develops from the first-cleft/first-arch region, not from the tubotympanic recess of the pouch.
rationales.c: The internal auditory meatus is a bony canal associated with the otic region and is not a derivative of the tubotympanic recess.
rationales.d: The facial canal is a bony passage for the facial nerve and is not formed by the first-pouch tubotympanic recess.

marrow__ANAT_CH08_Q014.takeaway: The membranous labyrinth derives from the otic vesicle formed by invagination of the surface-ectodermal otic placode.
marrow__ANAT_CH08_Q014.displayText:
The membranous labyrinth of the inner ear is derived from the otic vesicle.

The surface ectoderm on either side of the hindbrain thickens to form otic placodes. The otic placodes invaginate to form otic vesicles (auditory vesicles).

The otic vesicle further divides into 2 components that develop into structures of the membranous labyrinth:
• The ventral component forms the saccule and cochlear duct
• The dorsal component forms the utricle, semicircular canals, and endolymphatic duct

rationales.a: The first pharyngeal pouch forms the tubotympanic recess and contributes to the middle ear and auditory tube, not the membranous labyrinth.
rationales.b: The first pharyngeal cleft is associated with the external auditory meatus and outer tympanic-membrane layer, not the inner-ear labyrinth.
rationales.d: Meckel's cartilage is a first-arch cartilage related to mandibular and middle-ear derivatives and does not form the membranous labyrinth.
